entries.answer: Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot regulate blood glucose properly, and the version people mean by the word without a qualifier is type 2. The mechanism is insulin resistance: the cells stop responding properly to the hormone that moves glucose out of the blood, the pancreas compensates by producing more, and eventually it cannot keep up. Type 1 is a different disease with a similar name: the insulin-producing cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process, usually in childhood, and it requires lifelong insulin from the start. The distinction matters because the two have nothing to do with each other's cause and the treatments are opposites in emphasis. Untreated, either version damages blood vessels, and the complications that matter are to the kidneys, the nerves and the eyes, which is why the standard checks are a urine test for protein and an eye screening rather than only a blood sugar reading. It is a long-term condition that is controllable rather than curable, and weight, diet, activity and medication all move the outcome.

patterns: what happens during an asthma attack
entries.answer: Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways narrow and swell and produce extra mucus, making breathing harder and causing coughing, wheezing and chest tightness. The narrowing is usually driven by an immune response to a trigger, so the same person can breathe normally all day and badly in one moment: common triggers are allergens such as dust mites and pollen, cold air, exercise, smoke, viral infection and strong emotion. Because it is episodic, the diagnostic test is a spirometry that is normal between attacks, and the guideline approach is to give a reliever inhaler for when symptoms appear and a preventer inhaler used daily whether or not anyone feels unwell, since the inflammation is present even when the breathing feels fine. The serious risk is a severe attack where the person cannot finish a sentence, and the inhaled medicine acts within minutes by relaxing the muscle around the airway rather than by reducing the swelling. Untreated asthma is one of the commonest causes of emergency hospital admission in children, and most of those admissions are preventable.

patterns: how is high blood pressure treated
entries.answer: Hypertension is persistently raised blood pressure, and the word persistently is the whole diagnosis: one high reading in a clinic means nothing, since pain, anxiety, caffeine and a full bladder all raise it, and the definition requires elevated readings on more than one occasion. Blood pressure is written as two numbers, systolic over diastolic, measuring the pressure when the heart contracts and when it relaxes, and the usual threshold for treatment in adults is around 140 over 90. It is called the silent killer because it produces no symptoms for years while quietly damaging blood vessels, and the damage shows up later as stroke, heart disease, kidney failure and vision loss. The causes are mostly not mysterious: it rises with age, with salt intake, with being overweight, with little physical activity, with smoking and with a family history, and a minority of cases are secondary to another condition such as kidney disease. The treatment combines lifestyle, where reducing sodium, losing weight and exercising produce real reductions, with medication, and the measurement itself is the intervention since most people do not know their own number.

entries.answer: An infection is what happens when a microorganism gets past the body's defences and multiplies, and the terms people use loosely, such as catching a cold, are really describing different routes of entry. Bacteria and viruses are the two common groups and they behave very differently: bacteria are independent organisms with their own metabolism, which is why antibiotics work on them, while a virus is not alive by most definitions and can only reproduce inside a host cell, which is why antibiotics do nothing for one. The competing defences are physical, such as skin and mucus, the innate immune response that acts fast and without recognising anything specific, and the adaptive response that produces antibodies and memory and is why you do not catch the same cold twice. Transmission happens through droplets, through surfaces less often than people assumed before the pandemic, through contaminated food and water, and through vectors such as mosquitoes. Prevention is unglamorous and effective: hand washing, ventilation, clean water, vaccination, and covering a cough.

entries.answer: Malaria is an infection caused by a parasite carried by mosquitoes, and the word is used in the Philippines often in a different sense, for a fever in general, which is a real source of confusion both for travellers and for diagnosis. The life cycle matters for understanding it: mosquitoes bite an infected person and take up the parasite, and roughly a week later that mosquito bites someone else and passes it on, so the mosquito is the carrier rather than the cause. The symptoms are a repeating fever with chills and sweating, and because a malaria parasite can lie dormant in the liver and relapse months later, a single course of tablets is not always enough. The serious cases involve the parasite affecting the brain, the blood cells or the kidneys, and the danger is greatest for children and for pregnant people, which is why prevention is aimed at them. The prevention that works is a combination of clearing standing water where mosquitoes breed, using repellent or treated nets, and taking preventive medicine where the disease is common.

patterns: what are the warning signs of dengue
entries.answer: Dengue is a viral illness carried by the same day-biting mosquito as the other diseases in this group, and it is the one that has grown most in the Philippines, with outbreaks now recorded in regions that did not have them twenty years ago. The virus infects a person and the mosquito passes it on, and the incubation is short, usually a few days to a week, so a person can be bitten and then become infectious while still feeling fine, which is a large part of why it spreads in a community. The danger is in what can follow the fever, and it is easy to dismiss because a normal dengue case is unremarkable apart from fever, aches and a rash. The serious form involves the platelets the body uses for clotting dropping, so the danger is bleeding, and warning signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the gums, and restlessness rather than just weakness. Anyone recovering from dengue must also avoid aspirin and ibuprofen, since they worsen the bleeding tendency, and the period after the fever passes is when the risk is highest.
